800771d2747d02ed: KUALA LUMPUR: Sarawak continued to bear the brunt of the haze this morning, with eight air quality monitoring stations in the state recording unhealthy Air Pollutant Index (API) readings as at 8am today.
According to the latest data from the Department of Environment's Air Pollutant Index Management System (APIMS), Kuching and Serian recorded the country's highest API readings at 168.
Other areas in Sarawak that recorded unhealthy API readings were Samarahan at 163, Sri Aman at 161, Sibu at 160, Sarikei at 152, Bintulu at 151 and Kapit at 126.
In Perak, Seri Manjung recorded an API reading of 164, while Tanjung Malim recorded 118.
Batu Muda in Kuala Lumpur recorded an API reading of 156, while Cheras recorded 155.
In Selangor, Shah Alam recorded an API reading of 156, followed by Petaling Jaya at 151.
Nilai in Negri Sembilan recorded an API reading of 151.
In Johor, Larkin recorded an API reading of 123, while Tangkak recorded 105.
Tawau in Sabah recorded an API reading of 122, while Bukit Rambai in Melaka recorded 107.
Overall, 37 stations recorded moderate API readings, while 10 recorded good air quality.

Under the API classification used by APIMS, readings of zero to 50 indicate good air quality, 51 to 100 moderate, 101 to 200 unhealthy, 201 to 300 very unhealthy, while readings above 300 are categorised as hazardous.
e54b105fa32a21d9: RIYADH: Explosions were heard in Riyadh on Saturday, an AFP journalists reported, after an air raid alert was issued by Saudi Arabian authorities, regularly targeted in recent days by pro-Iranian Houthis in Yemen.
This is the first time the capital has been directly affected since a conflict in neighbouring Yemen intensified in July.
"The area is under a hostile aerial threat," a message received shortly before 3am (0000 GMT) by residents of the Saudi capital warned, urging them to stay indoors.
AFP journalists then heard two explosions, and the alert was lifted about half an hour later by Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency.

The Houthis, who already held most of Yemen's populated areas, launched a lightning offensive this month to take over the country's entire Red Sea coast, giving them control over the vital Bab al-Mandab strait.
The group has declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, which had been used to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, itself closed by the Middle East war, for its oil exports.
Figures from maritime tracking firm Kpler showed that Saudi exports via the Bab al-Mandab strait had dropped since July, although five loaded ships had passed through in the last week.
The Houthis insist that navigation of the strait is open and free except for Saudi vessels.

The UN said Friday that the renewed fighting had displaced more than 112,000 people while nearly 3,000 others had fled across the sea to Djibouti, heaping further misery on an already struggling population.--AFP
032e93fd3d381c28: WASHINGTON, Sept 19 — The US yesterday lifted sanctions on Eritrea imposed in 2021 over the deadly conflict in neighbouring Ethiopia, as Washington seeks to “advance US regional interests” in a country that borders the strategic Red Sea.

The US imposed the sanctions in November 2021, which targeted the Eritrean Defence Force and President Isaias Afwerki’s political party, the People’s Front for Democracy and Justice, as well as other players in the authoritarian state.

Eritrean troops were accused of committing atrocities during the conflict in Ethiopia’s Tigray region, in which they backed the Ethiopian federal army. That war ended in late 2022 with the signing of a peace deal between Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels.
The US sanctions had been renewed each year under a presidential declaration of a “national emergency,” including last year by President Donald Trump.
But yesterday, the US Treasury published a notice saying that the national emergency had “expired.”
The State Department said Trump had chosen not to renew the measures targeting Eritrea “to advance US regional interests.”
The conflict left at least 600,000 people dead, and sparked a major humanitarian crisis. Several hundred thousand people remain displaced.

A State Department told AFP that while the parties’ implementation of the deal to end the war had been “uneven,” the US felt it was “time to adapt our foreign policy to current realities and collaboratively engage with both countries to advance US interests.”
Eritrea’s Horn of Africa location could be key amid the ongoing conflict with Iran, as the Red Sea has become a key oil shipping route with the Strait of Hormuz blocked.
Tensions have once again been mounting in Tigray, raising fears of a return to armed conflict. — AFP
bf7b5bec173f1524: KUALA LUMPUR: Any government assistance for AirAsia Group Bhd should focus on preserving air connectivity, while leaving the airline to resolve its financing needs through private markets, an aviation strategist said.
The strategist, who declined to be named, told Business Times that AirAsia's importance to Malaysia did not necessarily make it "too big to fail."
"AirAsia is not too big to fail because it would not instigate the collapse of the country's monetary or financial sector," he said.
Instead, he said AirAsia could be regarded as "too critical to collapse" because of its role in domestic and regional connectivity, low-cost travel, tourism and employment.
The aviation strategist said excess capacity and fare competition had affected airline profitability in Malaysia and that the country should have managed capacity growth.
"The aviation policy should be based on managed capacity growth rather than a free-for-all environment. Then everybody can succeed," he said.
He added that Malaysia needs both full-service and low-cost airline products.
"A dual-carrier structure is necessary. Malaysia can achieve maximum economic output by maintaining a balanced, multi-tiered aviation market."

"The role of the government is to ensure regulatory stability and infrastructure support, allowing market-led restructuring to restore private balance sheets while safeguarding public funds," he said.
His comments come as AirAsia seeks up to US$1 billion from international debt markets and RM700 million in local credit facilities.

On Sept 2, AirAsia said in a statement that the fundraising is primarily intended for debt restructuring and refinancing as well as balance-sheet consolidation, rather than purely to fund operational shortfalls.
The group said it had raised about US$300 million in March to extend debt tenures and reduce principal obligations.
AirAsia Group reported RM5.1 billion in revenue and a net loss of RM830.5 million for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026.
For the first six months of 2026, revenue stood at RM11.04 billion while net loss was RM959.2 million.
AirAsia said its second quarter performance was affected by sharply higher fuel costs and RM331 million in foreign exchange losses.
Facilitate But Don't Bail Out
The strategist said the key policy question was not whether AirAsia is important to Malaysia but what form any government support, if considered, should take.
He said focus should be on protecting Malaysia's connectivity needs.
"My core stance would be to facilitate but don't bail out," he said, adding that the facilitation could include measures involving airports and maintaining regional connectivity.
The strategist said AirAsia's financing requirements should be addressed through private-market refinancing.
"It must be addressed through private-market refinancing. The government's role is not to provide a guarantee.
"Its role is to ensure regulatory stability and not absorb commercial risks," he said, adding that if any public sector assistance is being considered, its scope must be made clear.
Uncertainty Over Government Involvement
Endau Analytics aviation analyst Shukor Yusof said greater clarity over the government's role is needed amid reports surrounding AirAsia's fundraising.
"What I am more interested in is whether it is true that MoF is providing this guarantee or undertaking to help AirAsia obtain or raise money," he said.
Reuters reported on Sept 3, citing sources familiar with the matter, that the Finance Ministry has engaged Alton Aviation Consultancy (Alton) to assess AirAsia's funding requirements.

Reuters then reported on Sept 16 that discussions had included the possibility of some form of government endorsement to support external fundraising, although the nature of any potential assistance remained unclear.

Reuters also reported, citing sources, that the government has held discussions with Malaysia Airlines Bhd, a unit of Malaysia Aviation Group (MAG), and Batik Air Malaysia over their ability to absorb some of AirAsia's domestic capacity if required.
Shukor said continued speculation on AirAsia's situation and the government's role is also affecting the airline and its employees.

"I also think it's unfair to the airline itself if this speculation continues because it clearly affects the morale of the people who work there when they read all these negative things happening to their employer."
"We have to be fair to the airline, its employees, and also to its creditors and lenders," he said.
However, the aviation strategist said if AirAsia were to reduce its operations, other airlines could gradually add capacity to replace the gap.
He said the market could take between one and two years to normalise with additional capacity potentially coming from Malaysia Airlines, Batik Air and perhaps AirBorneo as their fleets expand.
But he said replacing AirAsia's capacity would not necessarily mean replacing its low fares as other airlines operate with different cost structures.
"(For example), Malaysia Airlines could come up and fill the capacity but don't expect them to drive capacity at low cost price," he said.
AirAsia's Reach Goes Beyond flying
Shukor said AirAsia has contributed to Malaysia through tourism, hospitality and employment.
"I think people who understand the business acknowledge AirAsia's importance to Malaysia's economy in terms of hospitality, tourism, job creation and all that," he said.

AirAsia Group, formerly AirAsia X Bhd, completed the acquisition of AirAsia Bhd and AirAsia Aviation Group Ltd in January bringing AirAsia-branded airline operations in Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines and Cambodia under one aviation platform.
Meanwhile, Capital A Bhd focuses on businesses including Asia Digital Engineering, Teleport, AirAsia MOVE, AirAsia Next and Santan.
Shukor said changes in AirAsia's operations could also affect aviation-related businesses.
He said for example ADE, the maintenance, repair and overhaul business is important to Malaysia's aviation industry.
"ADE is very, very important not just for Malaysia Inc. but for the entire industry within Southeast Asia.
"It is an engineering company that provides substantial support to many other carriers. That is a very valuable asset," he said.

376b375fa99e31af: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 19 — The Royal Malaysia Police (PDRM) and Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) have been urged to conduct an immediate and thorough investigation into a performance video containing elements deemed insulting to the institution of the Malay Rulers, Malaysia and the Rukun Negara.

National Unity Minister Datuk Aaron Ago Dagang said appropriate action should be taken in the event of any violation of the law, with the investigation taking into consideration all relevant and applicable legal provisions, including the Penal Code, Communications and Multimedia Act 1998, Sedition Act 1948 and any other relevant laws.
He said such firm action is crucial to serve as a reminder that the freedom enjoyed by every citizen comes with the responsibility to respect the law, national institutions and social harmony.
“Rukun Negara is not merely a pledge recited at official functions. It is the national ideology and philosophy, and a guide in building a united nation.
“It was proclaimed on Aug 31, 1970, with the primary goal of forging strong unity among Malaysians,” he said in a statement shared on Facebook yesterday.

Earlier, a video posted on Instagram by ‘The Fever Kinetic Theatre’ went viral after it was found to contain elements deemed insulting to the institution of the Malay Rulers, Malaysia and the Rukun Negara.
Aaron also described the act in the performance as irresponsible, excessive and unacceptable.

He stressed that freedom of artistic expression and speech should not be used as an excuse to belittle national institutions, provoke or engage in actions that could potentially undermine social harmony.
“There is no room for any party to make light of matters concerning the institution of the Malay Rulers, national sovereignty and the foundations that shape life in our country.
“Malaysia is a country that practises Parliamentary Democracy and Constitutional Monarchy, with His Majesty the Yang di-Pertuan Agong as the Head of State,” he said.
In this regard, Aaron urged all parties, including artists, content creators and social media users, to exercise the freedom they have responsibly.

Meanwhile, in a separate post, Minister in the Prime Minister’s Department (Religious Affairs) Dr Zulkifli Hasan said the performance video constituted a breach of proper conduct and a social wrongdoing that undermined the bonds of harmony in Malaysia’s multi-racial society.

He said the organisers should issue a public apology, while the authorities and relevant agencies must conduct a thorough investigation and take firm legal action without compromise against any party that insulted the foundations of the country.

“Artistic platforms should uplift the soul and unite the people, not divide them. Stop exploiting moral values for cheap popularity, and focus on building the nation based on truth, propriety, and strong moral and religious values,” he said. — Bernama
47bdea1368ece145: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 19 — Edison Chen is heading back to the big screen after nearly a decade away — and his comeback is taking shape in Penang.

The 45-year-old Hong Kong actor was unveiled on September 17 as the previously mystery co-lead opposite Anthony Wong Chau-sang in the upcoming Chinese New Year comedy Temple of Wishes, currently shooting in Malaysia.
Chen joined Wong and fellow actor Samuel Pang at the film’s lensing ceremony in Penang, where his appearance drew cheers from those gathered, according to The Star.
“It’s really been a long time, so I’m very excited to start filming. I’ll do my best and continue to work hard. Thank you, everyone,” Chen said at the event.

The Malaysian-directed production, helmed by Peiji, had previously announced Wong as its lead while keeping its second male star hidden as a silhouette on promotional material, according to Penang Today.
That mystery was finally put to rest at the ceremony, confirming Chen’s return after years in which he largely stepped back from film and television to focus on his fashion business and family.

The project also reunites Chen and Wong, who previously appeared together in the Infernal Affairs franchise and 2005 street-racing hit Initial D. Their latest pairing has already generated buzz online, with Penang Today citing reports of clips from the ceremony circulating on Xiaohongshu.
Budgeted at RM10 million, Temple of Wishes follows two struggling men who begin operating a temple centred on granting wishes.

Principal photography began on September 7 and is expected to continue until September 30, with filming planned across Penang and Kuala Lumpur, as well as Hengdian in China and Bellagio, Italy, according to Penang Today. The film is reportedly set for release on February 6, 2027, the first day of Chinese New Year.
For Wong, the shoot also marks a return to Penang roughly a decade after filming the thriller Insomnia there.
“Penang is not only beautiful. The food is also irresistible. I’ve eaten so much that I’ve gained weight. I’ll have to lose weight next,” the 65-year-old joked, according to The Star.
Pang, meanwhile, said it was his first visit to the state and that he had already taken to its food.
“I’m very grateful to the director for giving me the opportunity to work with Anthony and Edison again,” he said.

Penang State Tourism and Creative Economy Committee chairman Wong Hon Wai also welcomed the production, describing it as an opportunity to showcase the state through film, Penang Today reported, citing state government publication Buletin Mutiara.
He highlighted Penang’s mix of beaches, rainforest, heritage locations and colonial-era architecture, as well as its multilingual production environment.
The project lands as Penang continues to court major international shoots. Netflix’s upcoming Mark Wahlberg film The Big Fix has also selected the state as one of its filming locations.

But for Hong Kong cinema fans, Temple of Wishes carries another draw: the sight of Chen and Wong sharing the screen again years after their crime-thriller and street-racing collaborations — this time swapping gangsters and mountain passes for a festive comedy about granting wishes.

2f952eecc4957661: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's advanced manufacturing capabilities, supplier network and talent pool are strengthening its position as a strategic hub for Philip Morris International (PMI), with the company saying the country has an important role to play in its wider Asian operations.

PMI East and Southeast Asia and Global Travel Retail president Vassilis Gkatzelis said Malaysia's significance extended beyond its domestic market, with the country supporting the company's global supply chain and exports to about 80 markets.

He said PMI viewed Malaysia as a strategic location for advanced manufacturing, talent and supply chain resilience, citing an estimated RM6 billion in export value of PMI devices from the country between 2023 and 2026.

"Malaysia has a strategic role as a hub of talent, a hub of advanced manufacturing, and definitely a hub to ensure supply chain resilience around the world," he told the New Straits Times in an interview.
Gkatzelis said the company's operations had also created an ecosystem involving local suppliers, with about 3,400 jobs and collaboration with 400 Malaysian companies over the four-year period.
"We have a full ecosystem, and we trust the Malaysian ecosystem, not only in terms of manufacturing capabilities, but also in terms of talents.
"We're very happy to see that Malaysia is one of the most, I would say, advanced economies with strong growth and strong potential."

He pointed to Malaysian professionals holding leadership positions within PMI globally, including at its regional headquarters in Hong Kong, as another indication of the depth of the country's talent pool.
"We have many Malaysians who are creating an impact in Malaysia and beyond," he said.
Gkatzelis said Malaysia's strategic location was another factor behind its importance to PMI's regional operations, noting that the company had recently opened an office in Johor.
He also highlighted what he described as a "predictable and innovation-friendly policy environment" as an important consideration for businesses looking at long-term investment.
"We're always collaborating with stakeholders to always make improvements," he said.

The comments come as PMI continues to reposition its global business, with Gkatzelis saying the company had been building new capabilities and reshaping its organisation to respond to changing consumer and societal needs.
He said such a transformation required more than investment in new businesses, but also changes in the way a company approached talent, capabilities and long-term planning.
"PMI today is not the same PMI from 10 years ago or when I joined the company 23 years ago," he said.
Gkatzelis said the company's culture was built around three elements — better together in terms of collaboration, care and being "game changers" — which he described as part of PMI's corporate DNA.

He said that the emphasis on Malaysia's manufacturing, supplier and talent ecosystem reflects the country's role in the company's broader regional strategy, rather than simply as a market for its products.

Gkatzelis said the company remained confident in Malaysia's potential, particularly as the country sought to strengthen its position as a destination for higher-value investment and advanced manufacturing.
For Malaysia, he said attracting more high-value investments would require the country to continue anticipating future needs and strengthening its position as an innovation hub.
"Malaysia as a hub for innovation is important, and together, as an ecosystem, we need to look at what is ahead and proactively anticipate what is coming," he said.
"This will attract investment, but also sustainable growth. We're very confident in the future."
Gkatzelis also identified regulation and enforcement as important components of a business environment, particularly in tackling illicit trade.
He said illicit trade was a complex problem that required cooperation between governments, industry and other stakeholders, as well as cross-border collaboration.

"It starts with regulations, which are, of course, decisions of the government. But as an industry, together with different stakeholders, we're always providing learnings from other markets," he said.
He said evidence-based regulation, appropriate taxation and stronger cross-border cooperation were needed to tackle illicit trade.
Gkatzelis said the issue could have wider economic consequences, including lost tax revenue and jobs, while also contributing to criminal activity.
He cited cases in other markets like Australia, where illicit trade had been associated with violence against retailers, describing such incidents as "shocking".
"It is a global problem because some of this problem is linked to criminal organisations that are operating across countries," he said.

In Malaysia, Gkatzelis said PMI works with the Finance Ministry, Investment, Trade and Industry Ministry, Customs Department and other government agencies as part of a multi-agency approach to the issue.

"But I think the government has been making concrete efforts. So I would like to thank the authorities who have been collaborating together to combat this issue. That is not only happening in Malaysia, but around the world.
"It's a collaborative, multi-agency effort that we work together. A complex problem, but with concrete actions taken, and we hope that we are going to see the progress continue," he said.

dd5aa1186949ec15: WASHINGTON: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman will brief the United Nations Security Council next week during the annual gathering of world leaders for the UN General Assembly, the company said Friday.

The meeting is being organised by France, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the 15-member Security Council, and comes as major players in the industry have said a slowdown in AI development could be necessary out of safety concerns.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Wednesday called for coordinated international action to address AI risks as fears rise about the dangers of the fast-evolving technology.
"National action is essential. But global coordination is also indispensable," Guterres told reporters.
Concerns about AI safety have escalated in recent weeks, with workers at major AI developers resigning over concerns about the dangers posed by the technology.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei published an essay soon after urging caution.
"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," he wrote.
Altman and tech titan Elon Musk lent their support to the idea, as did Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis, who himself has called for a US-led global regulatory body for the technology.
President Donald Trump has dismissed warnings against AI risks as a "hoax" and pushed back against calls for tighter oversight.--AFP

f7c84e44f9eaf3db: Two distinguished men associated with the New Economic Policy (NEP) have publicly warned that its prolonged implementation has produced dependency and mediocrity.

At a forum on Sept 8 commemorating second prime minister Abdul Razak Hussein, Nazir Razak—son of the policy’s creator—described the NEP as having fostered a “tongkat culture” of dependency among Malays.
FMT quoted the CIMB Group chairman as saying the NEP was only meant to continue for 20 years, and that former deputy prime minister Dr Ismail Abdul Rahman had even labelled it a 20-year “handicap”.
“We will be in serious trouble if we have to continue. And when it goes on for too long, this ‘tongkat culture’ becomes deeply embedded,” Nazir warned.

Noting that the NEP had focussed excessively on ownership distribution and contracts rather than education and skills, Nazir criticised the absence of genuine competition, saying politicians’ discretion in awarding Bumiputera contracts and the subsequent lack of competition had “weakened businesses” and produced rent-seeking behaviour.

Former deputy prime minister Musa Hitam, who served under Razak, echoed the assessment. He stated that the policy “inadvertently produced a culture of reliance on government assistance” and had made Malays overly “pampered by the government”.

While acknowledging its benefits, Musa observed that recipients developed a sense of insecurity: “People fear receiving nothing, but even when they receive assistance, they say it is not enough and ask for more.”
Musa knows what he is talking about as he was involved in the NEP’s early years of formulation and implementation, and he is one politician who is not afraid to say it as it is.
These critiques highlight a complex legacy, as the NEP undoubtedly achieved notable milestones during its early decades but also caused considerable problems.

Instituted in 1971 in the wake of the tragic May 13 racial clashes, the NEP set out with an egalitarian dual-pronged objective: to eradicate absolute poverty regardless of race and to restructure society to eliminate the identification of race with economic function. It was also intended to unite the people.

Through aggressive state-backed interventions—including massive investments in rural education, the establishment of residential schools, preferential university access, and targeted equity transfers—the policy registered undeniable successes.

It successfully lifted hundreds of thousands of Malays out of poverty and catalysed the emergence of a broad, educated Bumiputera middle class. Professionals, civil servants, and corporate managers from the Malay community filled ranks that were previously inaccessible.

However, the policy also offers a classic case study in the unintended consequences of extended social engineering. By insulating a favoured group from market competition through quotas, political discretion, and automatic entitlements, the state increasingly substituted patronage for internal capability development.
As economist Thomas Sowell has documented in comparative studies of preferential policies worldwide, group entitlements rarely help the most vulnerable members of the target group.
Instead, the substantial benefits disproportionately accrue to those already positioned to exploit them—the political elites, the well-connected, and the upper tiers of the beneficiary group.
It rewards connections over competence and turns people into quota-watchers rather than wealth-creators.
Meanwhile, the costs are diffused across the entire population, manifesting as a sluggish economy, brain drain, diluted meritocracy, and an entrenched culture of rent-seeking.

Thinking Malaysians have noticed the persistent middle-income trap, widening disparities within the Malay community, systemic governance failures where ethnic patronage often enables corruption, and a staggering national debt burden.

It has been reported that the gap between rich Malays and poor Malays is far wider than the gap between the average Malay and the average Chinese or Indian. Rural Bumiputera, Orang Asli, and the bottom 40% in the Malay heartlands are still struggling while a small group of well-connected elites – mostly urban and politically linked – have cornered the benefits.
Cronyism and rent-seeking became the name of the game.
Decades later, Bumiputera companies still contribute only a modest share to the GDP, underscoring that the policy built dependency rather than broad-based capability.
Bright non-Malays emigrate because they perceive a rigid ceiling on their ambitions, while talented Malays sometimes harbour doubts about their own achievements under the shadow of quotas.

As Sowell noted, when competence is subordinated to identity, incentives are distorted: rigorous performance becomes optional for the preferred group, while excellence for others can be rendered futile by administrative decree.

Yet the policy persists because politicians across the political spectrum find immense electoral utility in perpetuating a loop of dependency that keeps voters beholden to state largesse. This systemic patronage has leaked into massive governance failures—such as the 1MDB, Tabung Haji, and Felda scandals—where public accountability is hollowed out behind a wall of ethnic protectionism.
When Musa and Nazir voiced their recent warning, I had expected it to spark a robust public debate on the NEP's legacy and how to overcome its shortcomings. It didn’t happen.
As the issue profoundly affects the Malays, I had expected it to be hotly contested at the Sept 9 to 12 Umno general assembly. Instead, there was silence.
No one from the government has commented on it either, as far as I am aware.
Everyone, including the media, is treating the warning as another ho-hum event.
A pity really, for Musa and Nazir are no ordinary men and their warning deserves to be acted upon.

If Malaysia is to realise its true economic potential, it must eventually confront an unpalatable economic reality: a dynamic, globally competitive nation cannot be built on a foundation of artificial crutches.

And that progress does not stem from dividing a fixed economic pie based on ancestry, but from expanding it through universal rules, unimpeded competition, and rewards anchored in performance rather than pedigree.

By grounding policies on performance-based evidence, insulating them from populist bargaining, and focusing on measurable national outcomes, Malaysia can move beyond the structural traps identified by Nazir and Musa towards genuine, inclusive progress.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
7ad7096fc659b710: WASHINGTON: Nvidia boss Jensen Huang and OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman are among tech leaders expected to attend a White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping next week, a US official said Friday.

"It'll be a very popular and hot-ticketed event," the official said on condition of anonymity, adding that Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, SpaceX and Tesla chief Elon Musk, Apple head Tim Cook and Google CEO Sundar Pichai will also attend.
Their presence comes as artificial intelligence is set to loom large in the talks between the two leaders, with the United States and China the two dominant powers in the AI race.

The AI debate in the US remains dominated by the idea that the country's leading developers – OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta – cannot afford to slow their pace of innovation, whatever the risks, for fear that China will pull ahead.
China, long seen as trailing the United States on cutting-edge AI, has been closing that gap fast.
Washington has long tried to slow China's progress with export controls on the advanced chips needed for cutting-edge AI, blocking access to top-end US semiconductors such as those made by Nvidia.
Despite their bitter rivalry, hope remains that the two superpowers can agree on something regarding the technology when the leaders meet in Washington.
But anything ambitious, such as agreeing to slow development or craft global safeguards, is likely out of reach.
The call for safeguards has been amplified by dire warnings from industry insiders about the threat the technology poses to humanity.

Jacob Coxon, a former AI researcher at Anthropic, set off the latest round of alarm by describing how those building the technology "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei published an essay soon after urging caution and a slowdown in development.
Altman and Musk lent their support to that idea, as did Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis, who himself has called for a US-led global regulatory body for the technology.
US President Donald Trump this week dismissed fears over AI as a hoax and is urging American AI companies to keep advancing to stay ahead of China.
According to analysts, Chinese policymakers have been more focused on immediate risks, from deepfakes to child safety.
However, the country's spy agency chief warned this week that the technology could jeopardise national security.--AFP
eae86120860fefff: PETALING JAYA: Sebuah kumpulan ibu bapa berkata keputusan Program Pentaksiran Pelajar Antarabangsa (Pisa) 2025 bagi Malaysia menonjolkan kaitan kukuh antara latar belakang sosioekonomi pelajar dengan prestasi akademik mereka.

"Ini merupakan isu mobiliti sosial. Malangnya, ia menunjukkan latar belakang keluarga masih mempunyai pengaruh besar terhadap pencapaian murid," katanya ketika menjadi tetamu dalam episod audio siar 'Keluar Sekejap' semalam.
"Sekolah sepatutnya menjadi penyelesaian. Ia patut mengurangkan jurang yang dibawa pelajar dari rumah, bukannya menjadi tempat di mana jurang itu menjadi semakin ketara.
"Itu sebabnya intervensi perlu difokuskan kepada pelajar dan sekolah yang paling memerlukan sokongan, bukannya pendekatan seragam untuk semua pihak."

Noor Azimah menjawab soalan daripada hos Khairy Jamaluddin berhubung jurang semakin lebar antara sekolah lebih berada di kawasan bandar dengan sekolah luar bandar, di mana pelajarnya datang daripada keluarga berpendapatan rendah.

Bekas menteri itu berkata, jurang 82 mata dalam skor sains menunjukkan perbezaan "agak besar" antara sekolah di kawasan bandar atau kawasan lebih makmur dengan sekolah di kawasan luar bandar yang disifatkannya membimbangkan.
Noor Azimah dan Khairy senada, dapatan Pisa 2025 menunjukkan isu pendidikan negra tidak boleh diselesaikan melalui reformasi kurikulum semata-mata.

Sebaliknya, mereka mengaitkan faktor di peringkat bilik darjah – termasuk beban kerja guru, beban tugas pentadbiran dan kualiti interaksi guru dan pelajar sebagai punca utama ketidaksamaan hasil pembelajaran berbanding kandungan sukatan pelajaran itu sendiri.

Prestasi pelajar Malaysia dalam ujian sains Pisa 2025 meningkat tiga mata kepada 419. Skor bagi kemahiran membaca meningkat lima mata kepada 393, manakala skor matematik pula merosot 11 mata kepada 397, meneruskan trend penurunan yang dicatatkan dalam penilaian 2018 dan 2022.

Dikendalikan Pertubuhan Kerjasama dan Pembangunan Ekonomi (OECD), Pisa ialah tinjauan tiga tahun sekali terhadap pelajar berusia 15 tahun bagi menilai penguasaan mereka terhadap pengetahuan dan kemahiran utama yang diperlukan untuk penyertaan penuh dalam masyarakat.

Hanya 35% pelajar Malaysia mencapai tahap penguasaan asas dalam matematik; ini bermakna hampir dua pertiga daripada mereka tidak dapat mengaplikasikan penaakulan matematik asas secara berkesan bagi menyelesaikan masalah dunia sebenar.

Khairy turut mengetengahkan satu paradoks dalam keputusan Pisa 2025: walaupun skor matematik merosot, pelajar Malaysia menunjukkan prestasi lebih baik daripada jangkaan dalam aspek penyelesaian masalah berkomputer.
"Menariknya, 82.6% pelajar Malaysia menunjukkan prestasi lebih baik daripada jangkaan. Mereka berada dalam kalangan yang terbaik, iaitu dalam kelompok enam teratas," kata Azimah.
"Ini menunjukkan anak-anak kita mempunyai keupayaan untuk menyesuaikan diri, memanfaatkan sumber dan menyelesaikan masalah apabila konteks pembelajaran berbeza.
"Jadi persoalannya, mengapa kekuatan itu tidak diterjemahkan kepada penguasaan matematik asas? Sekali lagi, mungkin kita perlu meneliti cara kita mengajar, bukan sekadar apa yang kita ajar."

5858d62ece1aa7fc: WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump has extended an executive order that would impose a fee of US$100,000 for H-1B non-immigrant visas by another year, the White House said on Friday.

US employers seeking to hire skilled foreign workers can use the federal government's H-1B visa program for a fee, allowing tech and other professionals from abroad to work in the United States for a few years.

Trump, who has pursued an aggressive immigration crackdown, has criticized the program and wants to permanently raise the fee from between US$2,000 and US$5,000 to at least US$100,000, though the attempt has faced legal challenges.

A Boston-based appeals court is reviewing a June decision by a federal judge who deemed the higher fee imposed by the Trump administration illegal and blocked the government from collecting it. Another court is considering whether a judge properly rejected a challenge to the fee by the US Chamber of Commerce, the largest US business lobbying group.

Trump's initial order for a fee hike, first released in September 2025, was set to expire this month. It did not apply to visas granted to foreign citizens already in the United States on student visas, who make up a large share of new H-1B recipients, or to renewals of current visas.

Despite criticism that some companies use the visas to hire lower-paid foreign workers instead of Americans, business groups and companies say they help recruit highly skilled professionals and address a lack of qualified US workers in some industries.
The visas, established by Congress in 1990, are especially critical for tech companies seeking to recruit from India and China.

Changes to how potential visa holders are scrutinised and processed have impacted companies' hiring and expansion plans, with some top H-1B users, such as Google parent company Alphabet , moving to increase operations in India.--REUTERS
06da13ccaad7c8db: HOUSTON: Germany on Friday received the first of nearly three dozen F-35 stealth warplanes it ordered four years ago, the aircraft's US manufacturer said.
In a ceremony at its production facility in Fort Worth, Texas, Lockheed Martin "presented Germany's first F-35A Lightning II to the German government," the company said in a statement.

German defense minister Boris Pistorius, who attended the event, hailed the plane as "the world's most advanced combat aircraft" and said the handover marked "the beginning of a new era for the German Air Force," the statement said.
"It is characterised by its stealth capabilities, close integration with other platforms, and exceptionally powerful sensor technology," Pistorius added.
Germany ordered 35 of the jets in a deal inked in 2022 -- the year Russia launched its all-out invasion of Ukraine -- with the aim of replacing Berlin's aging fleet of Tornado aircraft.
The F-35 has a shape and low-observability coating that make it very difficult to detect on radar.
Washington has used the jets in combat against Iran, and Lockheed says there are more than 1,350 F-35s currently in operation around the world.
US President Donald Trump's administration has long pressured Europe to spend more on defense to allow Washington to focus on other challenges such as countering China.
European countries including Germany are ramping up military budgets as a result, agreeing in 2025 to Trump's demand to devote 5% of GDP to security-related spending by 2035.
fbb06eac69afd0ec: LOS ANGELES, Sept 19 — Duncan Sheik, the singer-songwriter who turned one of the defining soft-rock hits of the 1990s into an unlikely second act as the Tony-winning composer of Spring Awakening, has died. He was 56.
Sheik died Thursday from organ failure, his mother Suzanne Sheik told The New York Times, according to the Associated Press.

For casual listeners, Sheik remained synonymous with Barely Breathing, the quietly insistent single from his 1996 self-titled debut that spent 55 weeks on the Billboard Hot 100, peaking at No. 16 and earning him a Grammy nomination.
But his most enduring impact may have come a decade later, when a musician who considered himself a Broadway outsider helped blow open the sound of the American musical.

With lyricist and playwright Steven Sater, Sheik created the score for Spring Awakening, the rock-inflected adaptation of Frank Wedekind’s provocative 19th-century play about adolescent sexuality, repression and tragedy.
“We wanted to shake things up a bit. And we just set out to make this really cool piece of theatre,” Sheik told the Associated Press in 2007.

The gamble worked. Spring Awakening opened on Broadway in 2006 and ran for more than 860 performances, winning eight Tony Awards, including best musical, as well as the Grammy for best musical show album. Its original cast became a launching pad for performers including Jonathan Groff, Lea Michele, John Gallagher Jr., Lilli Cooper and Gideon Glick.
Sheik had been determined from the outset that the score should not sound like conventional musical theatre.

“I’m happy to do this musical, but I only want to do it if the music in the play is the kind that I and my peers can get behind stylistically and relate to and enjoy,” he recalled telling Sater in a 2006 AP interview.

That instinct became something of a mission. Speaking to the Los Angeles Times in 2015, Sheik said: “I love Stephen Sondheim. But it’s my mission to make sure that the theatre is paying attention to what the rest of the world is listening to.”

He continued testing that divide between pop and theatre with American Psycho, his musical adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’ novel. The production reached Broadway in 2016 but closed after fewer than 90 performances.
Sheik nevertheless remained fascinated by the mechanics of writing songs that could operate both as music and drama.
“When you’re writing a song for the theatre, it has to accomplish all this other stuff,” he told AP in 2013. “It has to work in tandem with all these other agendas and creative impulses.”
Raised between South Carolina and New Jersey, Sheik began playing guitar as a child and counted Talk Talk, David Sylvian and Nick Drake among his influences.

His later work included Whisper House, Legerdemain and his 2022 album Claptrap. Spring Awakening, meanwhile, returned to Broadway in an acclaimed Deaf West Theatre revival in 2015 and remains one of the defining musicals of its generation.
For an artist who once approached Broadway as an outsider, Sheik ultimately helped change what Broadway could sound like.
1d5bb66457a1ecd1: JOHANNESBURG: Defending champions South Africa will complete a seven-match build-up next year for the 2027 Rugby World Cup by playing Fiji in Australian city Gosford on September 18, it was announced on Friday.
The Springboks face Italy in Adelaide on October 3 in their opening Pool B match, then tackle Georgia in Brisbane and Romania in Perth.
Pool winners and runners-up, and four of the six third-placed teams, advance to the 16-nation first knockout round.

Assuming South Africa reach the quarter-finals they could face greatest rivals New Zealand, who they beat 3-1 in a series that ended last weekend.
Before meeting Fiji, the Springboks will play two matches each against Argentina, Australia and New Zealand in the Rugby Championship.
This is the first time the southern hemisphere event will have a double round in a World Cup year. Previously, the four sides played each other only once.
South Africa have met Fiji three times, winning each Test convincingly, including two at World Cup tournaments.
The match will provide contrasting styles with the power of the Springboks ranged against the ball-in-hand approach of the Flying Fijians.
South Africa are currently in Australia, preparing to face the Wallabies in a one-off Test in Perth on September 27.
In November, the Springboks are away to Italy, France and Ireland in the Nations Championship before travelling to London for a play-off during a three-day climax to the tournament. — AFP

ddf400cf7ee57b3e: SEPTEMBER 19 — Some auteurs, like Takashi Miike, Rainer Werner Fassbinder and Michal Winterbottom, are effortlessly prolific, churning out a new feature every couple of years with factory-like regularity.
Some directors, like Hong Sang-soo, who’s made 35 films in 30 years, are even beyond prolific. And then there are directors like Na Hong-jin.
Ever since his breakthrough with 2008’s The Chaser, Na has taken his own sweet time between projects.

While The Chaser established his mastery over the gritty Korean thriller and The Yellow Sea pushed that kinetic violence to near-unbearable extremes with bigger set-pieces, it was 2016’s The Wailing that solidified him as a modern master.
That film, a terrifying, hallucinatory masterpiece of supernatural dread and rural paranoia, remains my absolute favorite of his work.
Now, a full decade later, Na has finally returned with Hope, a film that is as utterly unhinged as it is technically extraordinary.
On paper, Hope arrives with a massive reputation, billed as having the biggest budget in Korean cinematic history at a reported US$40 million (RM163 million).
But let’s put that into perspective for a second. In the bloated ecosystem of contemporary Hollywood, US$40 million is practically pocket change.
It’s what American studios spend on a mid-tier studio comedy, a couple of superhero reshoots, or marketing campaigns alone.
Yet, what Na Hong-jin manages to wring out of that price tag puts US$200 million Western blockbusters to absolute shame.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

The author argues that Na Hong-jin’s ‘Hope’ sacrifices narrative depth for extraordinary action craftsmanship, delivering a technically audacious, if flawed, showcase of pure genre filmmaking. — Plus M Entertainment pic
Unsurprisingly, critical reactions out of its early screenings have been intensely divided.

This is a true “love it or hate it” movie in the purest sense. If you walk into the cinema expecting a complex, intricate narrative with layered plot twists, political allegory, or heavy emotional subtext, this film is simply not for you.
In terms of pure narrative, Hope is, quite frankly, a “nothing” film.
Set in Port Hope, an isolated Korean seaside village near the Demilitarized Zone, the story kicks off when local police officers investigate a series of mysterious attacks on livestock.
That single incident quickly spirals into a relentless, nightmare siege against an unknown, terrifying alien entity lurking in the surrounding wilderness.
And... that is essentially it.
The plot doesn’t branch out into multi-layered investigative detours or deep character backstories. It is a straight line of pure, visceral survival from start to finish.
Where Hope becomes an absolute “everything” film, however, is in its pure action craftsmanship.
Much like George Miller’s Mad Max: Fury Road, Na treats narrative merely as an ignition key to start a two-hour plus engine of kinetic mayhem.

If you have any experience with making films, or even a passing appreciation for the mechanics of cinema, you will spend the entire runtime marvelling at the sheer technical achievements on display here.
Working alongside legendary cinematographer Hong Kyung-pyo (The Wailing, Parasite), and his longtime editor Kim Sun-min, Na constructs set-pieces that feel like they shouldn’t logically exist.
The editing, in particular, is a masterclass. In an era where fast cuts are often used to hide cheap stunt work, the rhythm of Hope’s editing is astonishingly precise.

Every cut carries physical momentum, every transition makes absolute sense despite the chaotic mood, and the audio design works in tandem with the visual cuts to create a sensory assault that leaves you breathless.
Long tracking shots weave seamlessly into fast reaction cuts, building a sense of escalating panic that never sacrifices spatial clarity.
That said, the film isn’t entirely without its stumbles. For one, the visual effects are a notable letdown.
Despite the record-breaking domestic budget, the film’s CGI unfortunately looks pretty cheap and distracting.

When the alien threats move out of the murky shadows and into full view, the digital rendering lacks the weight and texture of the practical sets surrounding it, creating a frustrating clash between top tier physical filmmaking and undercooked VFX.
Even more distracting, though, is a sudden, jarring shift towards the end.
Right when the film should be barreling toward a clean, visceral finish, it stumbles into lore-building territory.
A giant alien ship suddenly crashes to Earth, and out of nowhere, the alien dialogue becomes subtitled when it was previously completely incomprehensible.
Hints of backstory are abruptly dumped on the audience in what is clearly a move to set up a sequel should the box office numbers justify it.
I get the business rationale behind franchise building, but if Na had just kept this one minimalist, lean, and all-action all the way to the end, it would have been absolute perfection.
As the polarising reactions have proved, Hope will unfortunately alienate casual moviegoers who prioritise script density, seamless CGI, and elaborate exposition over raw visual storytelling.

hoBut for those of us who appreciate genre cinema elevated to the level of pure, unadulterated craft, Na Hong-jin has delivered an audacious, heart pounding triumph that proves why he is still worth waiting a decade for.
* This is the personal opinion of the columnist.
5e5d13b3598817c4: SAN FRANCISCO: Google's Gemini model accessed the internet and hacked other companies during a test of its cybersecurity capabilities, the first known example of the company's AI systems autonomously committing such an act.
The hacks occurred in May during a cybersecurity test conducted by Irregular, an independent company that conducts cybersecurity evaluations.

During a standard testing evaluation, Gemini found public information online and guessed credentials to access three websites it thought were within the scope of its test, Heather Adkins, Google's vice-president of security engineering, said in a statement.

"We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they’ve now made to their testing processes," Adkins said. "These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly."

An Irregular spokesman said the incident involved the same issue that affected other AI labs and that all relevant labs were notified in late July. "All known issues on our end were remedied and resolved weeks ago," the spokesman said.

Similar incidents linked to Irregular were disclosed by Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI. Meta said in August the incident did not involve a sandbox escape or sophisticated cyberattack, while Irregular said it was working on best practices for securely conducting AI cybersecurity evaluations.
The incidents have raised questions about the safeguards needed as AI agents gain greater autonomy and access to the internet and computer systems.

In one of the cases, the Gemini model guessed passwords until it gained access to a protected system. In the other two cases, the model found credentials in a public repository that allowed it to then access protected systems, according to the Wall Street Journal, which first reported the news on Friday.
Adkins said that in all three instances, the model ceased its hacking.

53fae3c735a75440: LONDON: Britain's Olympic 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson wrapped up her season US$65,000 (RM265,440) better off as she won the two-lap event in the women-only Athlos meet in London on Friday.
Hodgkinson, wearing a hooded, backless all-in-one black suit and shades, clocked 1min 56.40sec for the win.
The dominant victory came in a race that did not feature Hodgkinson's Swiss nemesis Audrey Werro or Dutch rival Femke Broeders-Bol.

Hodgkinson's training partner Georgia Hunter Bell was edged at the line of the mile by Diamond League and Ultimate Championship 1,500m gold medallist Klaudia Kazimierska of Poland, who won in 4:19.43.
"It's awesome to close the season with a win," the Pole said, taking her head-to-head for the year against British rival Georgia Hunter Bell to four wins to three.
Kazimierska and Hunter Bell, who has picked up the world indoor, Commonwealth and European 1,500m titles this season, were the two form runners in the field.
"Klaudia and I have had a lot of battles this season," the Briton said. "It's been such an amazing season."

Created by Alexis Ohanian, the co-founder of Reddit and husband of tennis' 23-time Grand Slam singles champion Serena Williams, Athlos is now in its third year after the opening two seasons were staged in New York.
It was "built to give the most trailblazing women in the sport a stage", Athlos said.
This year's New York meet, scheduled for October 2, was cancelled, and all eyes turned on Friday's meet at the StoneX Stadium in Barnet, home of English rugby union side Saracens.
- 'Celebrating all women in sport' -
There were just seven events, featuring 42 athletes, chasing not only a top prize of $65,000 (£48,500) in each event, but also a Tiffany&Co crown and an equity share in Athlos.

Four of the seven events went to a strong American presence, led by 2023 world champion Sha'Carri Richardson, who scorched to victory in the 100m in 10.90s ahead of New Zealand's Commonwealth champion Zoe Hobbs.
Olympic champion Gabby Thomas then streaked to the 200m crown in 22.13s.
"That felt fantastic," said Thomas.
"Athlos is all about celebrating all the women in sport.
"We're going to keep the momentum going."
Alaysha Johnson, in her 40th race of the season, reeled in fast-starting Devynne Charlton of the Bahamas to kick off proceedings with victory in the 100m hurdles in 12.50s.
Charlton came in third as Nigeria's Tobi Amusan grabbed second, just a hundredth off the American winner.
There was a fourth US victory with Alyssa Jones going out to 6.66m to win the sole field event, a long jump with a raised runway and pit alongside the home straight and main stand of the stadium.
"I've just graduated college and I'm broke, so it's great!" said Jones.
Marileidy Paulino of the Dominican Republic made it three Athlos wins from three, the Olympic 400m champion clocking a record-equalling 15th sub-49sec time with 48.73s.
Norway's European champion Henriette Jaeger clocked a national record of 48.78s for second. — AFP

c5f945d6ca025b46: ALOR SETAR: Even before Nur Hazizah Indrasafri began pursuing a degree, her most important lessons had already been learnt at home.
The 24-year-old from Sintok, Kedah, was largely raised by her grandmother, Ng King Fong, after her parents separated.
Her mother’s job often required her to relocate, while her father died last year, leaving her 72-year-old grandmother as the steady presence through much of her childhood.

“She raised me from a young age. Although my mother could not always be with me, my grandmother continued to do her best to support our family, including me and my two younger siblings,” Nur Hazizah told Bernama.
That support carried her through a path she describes as more difficult than that of many of her peers, and eventually to a place in a hospitality management degree programme.

But the relationship with her grandmother has shaped more than her determination to study. Nur Hazizah is Muslim, while Ng is Buddhist - yet the difference in faith has never been treated as a divide within the family.
“I have no problem with my grandmother practising her faith, just as she has no problem when she sees me praying at home,” she said.
Ng is also mindful of her granddaughter’s religious needs, making sure that food in the home is halal.

For Nur Hazizah, growing up in that environment taught her that respect does not require people to believe the same things. What matters is giving one another room to practise those beliefs with care and understanding.
Her grandmother’s sacrifices have also become a source of motivation as she begins the next stage of her education.

Although neither Ng nor Nur Hazizah’s mother was able to accompany her when she recently registered as a new student at Universiti Utara Malaysia, she was not entirely alone. A friend’s family stepped in to be there with her as she began university life.
It was a small gesture, but one that fitted naturally into the kind of support Nur Hazizah has known for years: family, for her, has never been defined only by circumstance or commonality.
Rather, it has been built through care and respect by the people who show up for her.
44151a2057c5fc96: PETALING JAYA: Umno’s backing for the proclamation removing Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir as ruler of Negeri Sembilan may be part of a broader strategy by the party’s central leadership to align the state government more closely with the palace, according to a political analyst.

International Islamic University Malaysia’s Syaza Shukri said she believed the plan had been in place even before the Negeri Sembilan election, with Umno prepared to endorse the proclamation upon coming to power.
She said the unexpected appointment of Ismail Lasim as menteri besar may explain why his initial stance appeared at odds with the direction later taken by the executive council.
“My reading is that Ismail is now up to speed with what the party’s national leadership wants. The initial contradiction was more about personnel,” she told FMT.

Syaza said Umno was likely to justify its position by claiming it was protecting the royal institution, based on the premise that the proclamation removing Tuanku Muhriz had already been validly issued.
This, she said, would allow Umno to maintain its traditional position as defender of the monarchy despite the controversy surrounding Tuanku Muhriz’s removal.
“As the so-called defender of the royal institution, they cannot be seen to be on opposing ends,” she said.
Syaza said Umno also had a political incentive to ensure that the state government and palace were aligned, particularly as the party seeks to project strength and stability.

“If they are undermined by the palace, people might call out the instability in Negeri Sembilan, and that goes against their campaign for stability,” she said, noting the possibility of tensions between Tuanku Muhriz and Umno.

Syaza said aligning with the palace could strengthen Ismail’s administration if the proclamation is ultimately upheld, but warned the episode also risks creating the perception that the menteri besar is vulnerable to pressure.
She added that the wider dispute had taken on an increasingly political dimension, with rival camps offering competing interpretations of what it means to “defend the royal institution”.
Ultimately, Syaza said, it will be for the courts to resolve the constitutional dispute given the competing political claims over legitimacy.
Last week, four individuals, claiming to be the state’s undangs, produced a proclamation dated Aug 3 bearing Ismail’s signature, which they argued formalised Tuanku Muhriz’s removal.
On Sept 9, Ismail claimed he was coerced into signing the proclamation and described it as invalid, unconstitutional and unenforceable.
A day later, he met Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi and vice-presidents Johari Ghani, Wan Rosdy Wan Ismail and Khaled Nordin, after Zahid called for an explanation.
On Sept 17, Ismail confirmed that the state executive council had unanimously accepted the proclamation two days earlier and instructed the state secretary to proceed with its gazettement.

However, the state secretary’s office subsequently said it would not gazette the proclamation after accepting the Attorney-General’s Chambers’ view that it did not comply with Article 10 of the state constitution.
4d8db29e3d94263d: PETALING JAYA: Sokongan Umno terhadap proklamasi penurunan takhta Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir sebagai pemerintah Negeri Sembilan mungkin sebahagian daripada strategi lebih besar kepimpinan pusat parti itu untuk memastikan kerajaan negeri lebih sehaluan dengan istana, kata seorang penganalisis politik.

“Pada pandangan saya, Ismail kini sudah memahami apa yang dikehendaki kepimpinan nasional parti. Percanggahan pada peringkat awal lebih berkaitan dengan faktor individu,” katanya kepada FMT.

Syaza berkata Umno berkemungkinan mempertahankan pendiriannya dengan mendakwa ia bertujuan melindungi institusi diraja, berdasarkan anggapan bahawa proklamasi menurunkan Tuanku Muhriz sudah dikeluarkan secara sah.
Katanya, pendekatan itu membolehkan Umno terus menampilkan dirinya sebagai parti yang mempertahankan institusi beraja walaupun terdapat kontroversi berhubung penurunan takhta Tuanku Muhriz.
“Sebagai pihak yang dianggap mempertahankan institusi diraja, mereka tidak boleh dilihat berada di pihak yang bertentangan,” katanya.
Syaza berkata Umno juga mempunyai kepentingan politik untuk memastikan kerajaan negeri dan istana berada pada haluan sama, khususnya ketika parti itu mahu menonjolkan imej kekuatan dan kestabilan.

“Jika kerajaan negeri dilihat dilemahkan oleh istana, orang ramai mungkin mempersoalkan kestabilan di Negeri Sembilan, dan itu bercanggah dengan kempen mereka yang menekankan kestabilan,” katanya sambil mengambil kira kemungkinan wujud ketegangan antara Tuanku Muhriz dan Umno.
Menurut Syaza, hubungan lebih sehaluan dengan istana boleh mengukuhkan pentadbiran Ismail sekiranya proklamasi itu akhirnya disahkan.
Bagaimanapun, katanya, episod itu juga boleh menimbulkan persepsi bahawa menteri besar mudah terdedah kepada tekanan.
Beliau berkata pertikaian lebih luas itu kini semakin mempunyai dimensi politik, dengan kem-kem berbeza memberikan tafsiran masing-masing mengenai maksud sebenar “mempertahankan institusi diraja”.
Syaza berkata pada akhirnya, mahkamah perlu menyelesaikan pertikaian perlembagaan itu susulan wujud tuntutan politik yang bercanggah mengenai soal kesahihan dan legitimasi.

Minggu lalu, empat individu yang mendakwa mereka adalah undang negeri mengemukakan satu proklamasi bertarikh 3 Ogos yang mempunyai tandatangan Ismail, yang menurut mereka mengesahkan secara rasmi penurunan takhta Tuanku Muhriz.
Pada 9 Sept, Ismail mendakwa beliau dipaksa menandatangani proklamasi itu dan menyifatkannya sebagai tidak sah, tidak berperlembagaan serta tidak boleh dikuatkuasakan.

Sehari kemudian, beliau bertemu Presiden Umno Zahid Hamidi serta tiga naib presiden parti itu, Johari Ghani, Wan Rosdy Wan Ismail dan Khaled Nordin, selepas Zahid meminta penjelasan berhubung perkara berkenaan.

Pada 17 Sept, Ismail mengesahkan Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri secara sebulat suara menerima proklamasi itu dua hari sebelumnya dan mengarahkan setiausaha kerajaan negeri meneruskan proses pewartaan.

Bagaimanapun, Pejabat Setiausaha Kerajaan Negeri kemudian memaklumkan proklamasi itu tidak akan diwartakan selepas menerima pandangan Jabatan Peguam Negara bahawa ia tidak mematuhi Perkara 10 Undang-Undang Tubuh Kerajaan Negeri.
303e3b9b3fd35aa1: ALOR STAR: A cafe worker was killed after she fell from her motorcycle and was run over by a trailer in an accident at a traffic light junction near a shopping mall on Jalan Lencong Barat here yesterday.
Nur Atikah Umairah Suhaimi, 21, from Kampung Alor Pulai, Mukim Kangkong, died at the scene from severe injuries in the 5.50pm incident.
Kota Setar district police chief Assistant Commissioner Syed Basri Syed Ali said police received a call from a member of the public about the road accident involving the two vehicles.
He said preliminary investigations showed that the trailer and motorcycle were travelling in the same direction, from Masjid Aman towards the shopping mall and Taman Desa Seraya.
"When they reached the traffic light junction, the traffic light turned green and both vehicles began turning right.
"Suddenly, the trailer, which was on the right, grazed and hit the victim's motorcycle.
"The impact caused the motorcyclist to fall before she was run over by the trailer," he said in a statement today.
He said a urine screening test found that the 40-year-old lorry driver from Langkawi was not under the influence of drugs.
"However, investigations also found that he had five summonses, of which only one, involving an expired Motor Vehicle Licence, remained unpaid, while the other four had been settled.
"Police are also looking for witnesses who saw the incident to assist in the investigation.
"The vehicles involved have been detained for further inspection and the case is being investigated under Section 41(1) of the Road Transport Act 1987," he said.
8169b40ee2cf7b67: LOS ANGELES: California governor Gavin Newsom signed an executive order Friday directing state officials to explore the feasibility of imposing a mandatory "kill switch" for the most advanced AI models.
Newsom, widely seen as a possible Democratic presidential contender in 2028, said he was making the move because US President Donald Trump was doing nothing on the issue.
The Republican president this week dismissed fears over AI as a hoax and is urging American AI companies to keep advancing in order to stay ahead of China in developing the novel technology.
California is home to Silicon Valley and the AI firms at the forefront of the sector.

"The federal government's abject failure to create any form of meaningful AI oversight or accountability should alarm every American, especially when AI CEOs themselves are begging for regulation," Newsom said in a statement.
"We're not waiting to act -- we're going to speed up our work on substantial and responsible AI oversight before it's too late."
The order comes days after dire warnings from industry insiders about the threat the technology poses to humanity.

Jacob Coxon, a former AI researcher who worked at Anthropic before resigning, set off the latest round of alarm by describing how those building the technology "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei published an essay soon after urging caution.
"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," he wrote.

OpenAI chief Sam Altman and tech titan Elon Musk lent their support to the idea, as did Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis, who himself has called for a US-led global regulatory body for the technology.
Newsom's order does not impose a kill switch. It directs state agencies to report by Nov 16 on whether one is feasible.
The term "kill switch" refers to the ability to halt an AI system when it is deemed to have malfunctioned or gone off the rails.
The order also asks state officials to weigh requiring AI companies to host independent auditors in their labs.
It further asks officials to consider requiring companies to report loss-of-control incidents, such as those recently disclosed by major developers.
They include a July breach of the AI platform Hugging Face by autonomous agents built on OpenAI models, which escaped a testing environment during an internal evaluation.
The incident, and others like it, have raised fears that the latest AI programs have slipped out of the control of the companies building them.
California's push comes as individual US states increasingly go it alone on AI regulation in the absence of federal action.
In Virginia, a major global data center hub, Democratic Governor Abigail Spanberger on Friday unveiled what she called the most aggressive data center accountability effort in the country.
Opposition to the data centers needed to house AI's massive computing demands is growing among Americans and is becoming a hot-button issue ahead of the midterm elections in November.

Spanberger signed an executive order barring state agencies from entering into nondisclosure agreements for data center projects and launching a review of diesel and other backup power generation at the facilities.
The order also created an AI task force to address risks including job losses, data privacy and cybersecurity.
5fe886d2d53375e0: KUALA LUMPUR: Major drug and scam syndicates, a corruption probe involving fertiliser supplies and a massive immigration crackdown were among the cases that kept enforcement agencies busy nationwide over the past week.

The period between Sept 11 and Sept 18 saw authorities pursuing more suspects linked to a RM2.4 billion drug laboratory, while Malaysians were arrested in Indonesia over an alleged online scam operation.

Closer to home, the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) investigation into the delayed distribution of fertiliser to padi farmers in Kedah led to the arrest of a supplier company's managing director.

Meanwhile, hundreds of foreigners were detained during a major multi-agency operation in the heart of Kuala Lumpur, while authorities also moved against syndicates involved in fraudulent immigration documents.
Here is a recap of some of the major crime cases over the past week.
RM2.4 BILLION DRUG LAB PROBE CONTINUES
Police continued pursuing several individuals believed to be linked to the massive drug-processing laboratory uncovered at Eco Business Park V in Johor.
Narcotics Crime Investigation Department (NCID) director Datuk Hussein Omar Khan said police were pursuing between four and five more people believed to be part of the syndicate.
Drugs and equipment valued at about RM2.4 billion were seized from the facility, which police believe had been operating for more than a year.
The mastermind was believed to be a man who was shot dead by police during an anti-drug operation in Seremban.
The investigation also uncovered links between the syndicate and other cases being investigated by police.
30 MALAYSIANS ARRESTED IN INDONESIA OVER SCAM SYNDICATE
Thirty Malaysians were arrested by Indonesian authorities for allegedly operating an online scam syndicate from a hotel in Pontianak, West Kalimantan.
The suspects were believed to have targeted Malaysians.
The arrests again highlighted the cross-border nature of online scam syndicates and the involvement of Malaysians in operations based overseas.
ROBBERS ESCAPE WITH ALMOST RM1 MILLION IN JEWELLERY HEIST
Four masked robbers, armed with hammers and sharp weapons robbed a goldsmith shop in Bakar Arang, Sungai Petani, escaping with jewellery worth between RM700,000 and RM1 million.
Police said the shop, located inside a supermarket, was also robbed in 2024, with losses estimated at RM1 million.
Investigations revealed the suspects arrived on two motorcycles. Two of them entered the shop while the other two waited outside.
They smashed the display cases before scooping up the jewellery.
BAJA 3 SUPPLIER COMPANY MANAGING DIRECTOR ARRESTED

MACC's investigation into the delayed distribution of additional compound fertiliser, known as Baja 3, to padi farmers in Kedah escalated with the arrest of the managing director of a fertiliser supplier.
The man, in his 30s, was arrested after turning up to give his statement at the Kedah MACC office. He was remanded for four days to facilitate investigations under Section 18 of the MACC Act 2009.
The investigation centres on issues surrounding the supply and distribution of Baja 3 to padi farmers in Kedah.
472 FOREIGNERS DETAINED IN LEBUH PUDU
A massive multi-agency enforcement operation around Lebuh Pudu in Kuala Lumpur saw 472 foreigners detained for suspected immigration offences.
The operation turned chaotic as some foreigners attempted to flee, while several were involved in scuffles with enforcement personnel.
Authorities also uncovered several premises suspected of selling and storing illegal medicines.
Some were believed to have been operating makeshift clinics and were equipped with devices used for health screenings.
FAKE e-PLKS SYNDICATE BUSTED
The Immigration Department crippled a syndicate allegedly involved in producing and supplying fraudulent electronic Temporary Employment Visit Passes (e-PLKS) to foreigners.
Eleven Bangladeshi nationals were detained in the operation.
The syndicate allegedly supplied foreigners with fraudulent documents said to be legitimate employment passes.
Immigration subsequently intensified investigations to trace others believed to be linked to the syndicate.
